look_here_first: LOW MAT of small smooth-edged KIDNEY-SHAPED leaves, each on a long upright petiole from a creeping/rooting stem. Follow the stem: leaves are ALTERNATE, not opposite. Turn leaves over to find a solitary tiny PALE GREEN or CREAM five-lobed flower, much shorter-stalked than the leaves. If distinguishing from another Dichondra, check the fruiting stalk: usually STRAIGHT or barely bent and the FIVE persistent sepals LONGER than the little two-lobed capsule. Do NOT rely on round leaves alone.

taxonomic_note: Accepted species name Dichondra carolinensis Michx. (Kew POWO and FNA). Dichondra repens var. carolinensis is an historical synonym, NOT evidence that all plants sold as D. repens are this native taxon. POWO calls it native to Texas at state level; county-level BONAP/NAPA target-zone classification remains intentionally deferred under current project rules. Do not merge records with Dichondra recurvata, D. micrantha or D. argentea.

best_field_traits: Prostrate stolon-forming perennial herb only a few cm high; many rounded kidney-shaped leaves on ascending petioles create the visual mat.
Leaves ALTERNATE along creeping stolons; blades simple, kidney-shaped (reniform), cleft/notched at the base, with an ENTIRE (untoothed) margin.
Several main PALMATE veins radiate from the notch/petiole junction rather than one single midrib.
Tiny solitary flower sits in a leaf axil usually below the leaf canopy; pale green/cream corolla with five short lobes, not a yellow composite head.
Green CALYX of five separate often hairy sepals persists as petals disappear and enlarges with maturing fruit.
Fruit matures into a tiny distinctly two-lobed dry capsule; in D. carolinensis its persistent sepals are generally noticeably longer than the capsule.
To separate close Dichondra look-alikes, a roughly straight/nonnodding pedicel in fruit is more useful than whether one leaf looks bigger or greener.
morphology_keys.growth_habit: Mat-forming or loose creeping cover, with subterranean/at-surface slender stolons rooting at nodes, leafy tips standing to approximately 5 cm in the central-Texas detailed specimen treatment. Often hidden amongst grass and leaf litter.
morphology_keys.life_cycle: Perennial herb, creeping and rooting along stolons.
morphology_keys.stem: Slender runners at or just beneath soil surface, occasional aboveground red-green hairy stems; local UT treatment notes two-armed strigose hairs on green organs, often not visible without a hand lens.
morphology_keys.leaf_arrangement: Helically ALTERNATE—one petiolate leaf per node, NOT true opposite pairs. Dense runners can make nearby petioles appear paired; physically trace one stem.
morphology_keys.leaves: Simple, kidney-shaped to suborbicular; rounded or slightly indented tip, deeply cordate/notched petiole base, smooth/ENTIRE margins, variable minute hairs. UT local specimens approximately 10–23 mm long by 10–30 mm wide; FNA broader 3–25 by 6–30 mm including extremes.
morphology_keys.leaf_venation: Palmate, several major veins (UT reports commonly 3, 5, or 7) diverging from the petiole base; veins conspicuous on underside when leaf is flipped.
morphology_keys.petiole: Long, upright/slightly oblique leaf stalk: FNA commonly 10–50 mm, sometimes to 105 mm; much longer than tiny flower stalk in typical specimens. Petiole is attached at the BASE notch, not centrally on the leaf blade.
morphology_keys.flower: One (occasionally two) small axillary 5-lobed corollas, pale green to creamy white, roughly 1.5–3 mm by FNA; petals fused into a shallow bell/cup, not an Asteraceae composite head. Five calyx lobes remain below.
morphology_keys.flower_stalk: Pedicel often ~8–20 mm in FNA (extremes ca. 4–42 mm), usually fairly straight or just gently nodding; UT local treatment 5–15 mm combined small stalk section. Flowers commonly under leaf canopy and may be hard to locate.
morphology_keys.sepals: Five green, usually hairy, persistent calyx lobes; FNA 1.5–3 mm at anthesis and ~3.5–5 mm by fruit stage, generally LONGER than fruits. The central fruits can be obscured by these expanding lobes.
morphology_keys.fruit: Small deeply two-lobed capsule with lobes splitting/separating at maturity. The papery fruit wall breaks irregularly. FNA reports fruits 2–3 mm long and 1.6–2 mm wide (different source/whole fruit measurements may differ); local UT treatment about 3 by 5 mm. Do not use an exact millimeter cutoff without a measured fruit.
morphology_keys.habitat: Thin turf, disturbed lawns and compact path shoulders, lightly shaded beds, moist/open woods; UT Williamson County details support Central Texas field use. Ecology favors creeping mat over large upright stems.
morphology_keys.season: Warm spells and sufficient moisture favor visible fresh shoots and flowers; FNA lists flowering year-round across its full geographic range, not a Central Texas promise.
morphology_keys.key_cautions: Dichondra has tiny nonshowy flowers and is an exception to the large funnel-bloom 'morning glory' mental image. Leaves alone establish Dichondra-like identity, not certainty for D. carolinensis versus D. recurvata / introduced D. micrantha. Never assume commercial 'Dichondra repens' labeling confirms native identity.

comparisons.key_distinctions: D. recurvata: often significantly larger blades (typically ~20–30 × 30–40 mm) and larger corolla (~3–4 mm); most important, fruiting pedicel clearly bends backward at tip vs D. carolinensis usually straight, and sepals are shorter relative to fruit. D. micrantha: introduced species can look nearly identical; fruiting pedicel recurves and fruiting sepals only about 2–2.5 mm vs longer 3.5–5 mm in D. carolinensis. D. argentea: silvery densely hairy leaves, rather than green with lighter/scattered silky hairs. Dollarweed (Hydrocotyle): often round peltate blades (petiole attaching inside the underside), crenate edges and umbel-type tiny flowers; Dichondra petiole attaches at basal notch and entire margin. Straggler daisy: opposite small toothed leaves and tiny YELLOW composite flower heads. Frogfruit: opposite leaves generally toothed toward tip and clustered pale button inflorescence on a long stalk.

ecological_notes.habitat: Spreading perennial in thin warm-season turf, shaded/part-shaded moist or disturbed soil and edges of woodland; preserves low cover when not heavily disturbed.
ecological_notes.native_range: Kew POWO lists native to Texas at state level. BONAP local target-county native verification intentionally not undertaken in this finished-photo pass.
ecological_notes.insect_interactions: Native Plant Society of Texas lists pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) as a larval host association; do not infer species-level Lepidoptera host totals or specialty-bee counts without linked datasets.
ecological_notes.restoration_use: Useful to recognize in field restoration and distinguish from invaders, but not a stand-in for taller diverse forb/grass structure. Confirm provenance before sourcing.

family_genus_teaching.family: Convolvulaceae—same morning-glory family as Ipomoea, but Dichondra flowers are tiny and not trumpet-sized. Five small fused corolla lobes surround the flower; unlike composite Asteraceae heads.
family_genus_teaching.genus: Dichondra—creeping often rooting runners, alternate smooth kidney-shaped leaves and small solitary cream/green axillary flowers with two-lobed capsules; distinguish species by pedicel curvature, size, sepals, hairs.
family_genus_teaching.species: D. carolinensis—green kidney-shaped leaves with more scattered hairs; fruit stalk generally straight and sepals longer than fruit, unlike recurved-stalk D. micrantha and D. recurvata.
family_genus_teaching.crew_question: Can you trace one runner to prove leaves alternate, then flip the leaf and find the tiny green flower or two-lobed fruit below?
